CausalChain: Hypoxia -> Activation of HIFs -> Upregulation of PHGDH -> Enhanced serine synthesis pathway and folate cycle -> Increased NADPH production -> Effective ROS detoxification -> Tumor cell survival and drug resistance + Maintenance of immunosuppressive TME -> Impaired anti-tumor immune response; Inhibition of PHGDH -> Disrupted NADPH supply -> Elevated ROS -> Tumor cell death and immunogenic release -> Enhanced T cell activation -> Synergy with immune checkpoint inhibition.
Hypothesis: Selective inhibition of PHGDH in hypoxic HCC cells will compromise their redox homeostasis by reducing NADPH production, thereby augmenting ROS-induced immunogenic cell death and sensitizing these tumors to immune checkpoint inhibitors without significantly impairing effector T cell metabolism.
Abstract: Hypoxic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells adapt to oxygen deprivation by activating a hypoxia‐inducible factor (HIF)‐mediated metabolic reprogramming that enhances glycolysis, shunts metabolites into the serine synthesis pathway (SSP) and folate cycle, and suppresses mitochondrial function to limit reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. This metabolic adaptation contributes not only to robust survival under hypoxia but also to the emergence of drug resistance against tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Meanwhile, this reprogramming supports an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) via the accumulation of immunomodulatory metabolites such as lactate and adenosine. Here, we propose that selective targeting of the SSP through inhibition of phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), a critical effector of NADPH production in hypoxic HCC cells, will disrupt the redox balance in these tumor cells and promote immunogenic cell death. This process may simultaneously enhance the efficacy of ICIs by relieving the metabolic suppression imposed on tumor‐infiltrating lymphocytes, while sparing the glycolysis‐dependent metabolism of effector T cells. Combining selective PHGDH inhibition with ICI treatment may therefore overcome drug resistance in hypoxic HCC, offering a promising therapeutic avenue.
